opus-5.5.text:
Oh, I have a real soft spot for that paper. That was Branavan's work with Regina and David Silver, "Learning to Win by Reading Manuals in a Monte-Carlo Framework." Branavan was a few years ahead of me in Regina's group, so I saw a lot of that line of thinking up close, and it shaped how I thought about language for a long time.

What I loved about it was the framing. The agent isn't told what the manual means. It just has the text and the game, and it has to figure out which sentences are relevant to its current situation, and how, purely from whether using that information helps it win. Language understanding was grounded in control, in outcomes, rather than in annotated labels. In 2011 that was a fairly radical way to think about meaning. Most NLP then was about predicting labels on a fixed dataset, and here was this idea that you understand text if it helps you act better in the world.

And the results were striking. Reading the manual gave a big jump in win rate against the built-in AI in Civilization II. It showed that even fairly noisy, general text could carry useful prior knowledge for decision-making.

It directly influenced my own PhD work. Some of my early projects on text-based games, and on using language to help agents transfer across environments, came straight out of that question: can agents learn to read in service of acting? Looking back, it's interesting to see how the field has come full circle. Now we have large language models that already carry a huge amount of "manual knowledge," and the question has shifted from "can an agent learn to read the manual?" to "how do we get these models that have read everything to actually act well in an environment?" Language agents, tool use, web agents, all of that is in some sense a descendant of that line of thinking. So I'd say it was ahead of its time, and it's aged really well.

r001.rationale: The response says that reading the manual improved win rate in Civilization II and describes the agent using text to make better decisions, showing how language can improve an acting agent.

fable-5.1.text:
Oh, I have a real soft spot for that paper. That's Branavan's work with David Silver and Regina, from around 2011, and it was actually one of the papers that pulled me into the whole intersection of language and decision-making. I was Regina's student a few years after Branavan, so it was very much part of the lab lore by the time I showed up.

What I loved about it was the ambition. Everyone at that time was doing language grounding on very constrained setups, like mapping instructions to a few actions in a toy world. And here they were saying, let's take Civilization, a game with this enormous state space, hand the agent the actual game manual, and see if reading it helps you win. And it did. The agent that could attend to relevant sentences in the manual beat the agent that couldn't, by a pretty meaningful margin. That was a genuinely surprising result for the time.

The technical idea was also elegant. The text wasn't being parsed into some formal representation first. The model learned which parts of the manual were relevant to the current game state as a byproduct of trying to win. Language understanding was emerging from the reward signal rather than from supervised annotation. In hindsight, that's a very modern way of thinking about it. You can draw a line from that to the text-based game work I did later, and honestly to a lot of what people now call agents, where a model reads documentation or a tool description and acts on it.

If I'm being critical, the components were all fairly hand-engineered compared to what we'd do now, and the Monte Carlo search was doing a lot of the heavy lifting. The language model piece was comparatively thin. But that's a comment about 2011, not about the idea. The idea was right, and it was early. I'd put it on the list of papers that quietly shaped where the field ended up going.

r001.rationale: The response says the Civilization agent that used relevant manual text outperformed the agent that could not, and explains that it learned from reward while trying to win. This communicates that natural-language processing improved the reinforcement-learning agent.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a really interesting example of using language to help an agent make decisions. A game manual contains knowledge about how the world works and what strategies might be useful. The challenge is connecting those descriptions to what the agent actually sees and the actions it can take.

What I find exciting is the possibility of learning from both text and experience. Instead of discovering everything through trial and error, an agent can use what someone has written to guide its exploration, then refine that understanding by playing.

r001.rationale: It describes using language from the manual to guide an agent’s exploration and decisions, then refining its understanding through play and experience, conveying language-assisted reinforcement learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that was a really interesting piece of work because it showed that language could actually help an agent make decisions. A game manual contains knowledge about how the world works and what strategies might be useful. The challenge is connecting those descriptions to the situations and actions the agent encounters in the game.

What I find compelling is the broader idea: an agent shouldn’t have to learn everything through trial and error. If we’ve already written down useful knowledge, can it read that and use it to learn more efficiently? That connection between language and action is a very exciting direction.

r001.rationale: The response says language can help an agent make decisions and learn more efficiently from written knowledge, but it does not clearly characterize the agent as a reinforcement-learning agent.
